content.text:
NVDA’s +5.05% episode was a fairly coherent risk-on advance, not a selloff/reversal: the stock rose +0.36% on Apr. 13, +3.80% on Apr. 14, and +1.20% on Apr. 15, closing at $198.87, with the rolling Apr. 13→Apr. 15 signal matching the full-window gain [1]. The largest daily leg lined up with a broad market rally: on Apr. 14, AP reported the S&P 500 rose 1.2% and the Nasdaq climbed 2.0% as hopes for renewed U.S.-Iran talks pushed oil lower, and on Apr. 15 the S&P 500 rose another 0.8% to a record while the Nasdaq gained 1.6% as ceasefire-extension hopes remained high [2], [3]. That fits the attribution’s very large market contribution: this was mostly a high-beta AI/mega-cap move in a sharply improving tape, with NVDA adding some company-specific upside.

The firm-specific component was plausibly helped by Nvidia’s Apr. 14 announcement of “NVIDIA Ising,” an open-source family of quantum-AI models for calibration and error correction, including claims of up to 2.5x faster and 3x more accurate decoding versus traditional approaches [4]. That is not a near-term earnings event, but it reinforced the market’s “Nvidia as AI infrastructure platform” narrative during a tape that was already rewarding growth. A second firm-specific headline was more ambiguous: Nvidia denied reports that it was in talks to buy a PC maker after rumors had lifted Dell and HP shares; the denial reduced M&A-overhang risk, but the evidence does not show that this was a primary positive catalyst for NVDA itself [5].

The industry signal is the least clean part of the story. Public data and commentary point to semiconductors being strong, not weak: MarketBeat wrote on Apr. 14 that SMH was up almost 23% year-to-date and near all-time highs, driven by accelerating AI infrastructure spending [6], while StockAnalysis shows SMH itself rose +1.48%, +1.95%, and +0.22% over Apr. 13–15 [7]. That conflicts with the regression’s negative industry attribution, so I would interpret the -39% industry contribution as a model/orthogonalized factor result—possibly semiconductor beta lagging the broader Nasdaq/SPY move or being netted against market exposure—rather than evidence of an observable chip-sector selloff. Overall evidence supports a market-led rally with Nvidia-specific AI-platform news as a secondary contributor, while the industry-drag attribution is only partially supported by public news.
